narr: Let's start with our first bug hunt problem from the loops section.
We're looking at a nested loop structure that seems to have an issue.

data.heading: Problem L9 — Infinite Inner Loop
steps: The inner loop increments i instead of j
j remains 1 forever
The condition j <= 3 is always true
i grows infinitely
The inner loop loops infinitely and messes up the outer counter
data.result: Fix: Change i++ to j++ in the inner loop header

narr: Here's a classic bug that traps many programmers.
The problem is that the inner loop is incrementing the wrong variable.
Instead of incrementing j, it's incrementing i.
This means j never changes and remains stuck at 1.
Since j is always 1, the condition j <= 3 is always true.
Meanwhile, i keeps growing without bound.
This creates an infinite loop that also messes up the outer counter.

data.heading: Fixed Code for L9

narr: The fix is simple but crucial.
Change the inner loop header to increment j instead of i.
This ensures both counters progress properly.

data.heading: Problem L10 — Finding 7 in a Grid
steps: The code listing is truncated in the original file
7 is in row 0, column 1
Expected output: "First 7 found in row 0"
Break only exits the innermost loop
To terminate after the first find, use a found flag or goto-exit
data.result: This problem tests understanding of break behavior in nested loops

narr: Now let's look at a truncated problem that tests our understanding of nested loops.
The code listing is incomplete, but we can still learn from it.
The grid contains a 7 in row 0, column 1.
The expected output should indicate the first occurrence.
The key lesson here is about how the break statement works.
Break only exits the innermost loop, not all nested loops.
To properly terminate after finding the first 7, you need a flag or goto statement.

data.title: Bug Hunt Pointers & Strings
data.subtitle: Common Errors in Pointer and String Operations

narr: Moving on to our next section: pointers and strings.
This section covers twelve common bugs in pointer and string operations.
All errors have been verified by compilation with gcc and running under Address Sanitizer.
Many involve undefined behavior that may manifest differently across environments.

data.heading: Problem P1 — Missing Null Terminator
steps: The array has exactly 5 cells for 5 letters
No space remains for the null terminator '\0'
printf("%s") continues reading memory until it encounters a zero byte
The output is unpredictable as it reads beyond the array
data.result: Fix by adding space for the null terminator: char s[6] = {'h', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o', '\0'};

narr: Our first pointer and string bug involves missing null terminators.
This array has exactly 5 characters but no space for the null terminator.
When printf with %s tries to print the string, it keeps reading memory.
It only stops when it happens to find a zero byte somewhere in memory.
This leads to unpredictable output and potential security issues.

data.heading: Fixed Code for P1

narr: The fix is to allocate space for the null terminator.
Either make the array one larger and add '\0' explicitly,
or let the compiler handle it by using a string literal.

data.heading: Problem P2 — sizeof on a Pointer
steps: s is a char pointer, not an array
sizeof(s) returns the size of the pointer itself
On a 64-bit machine, this is 8 bytes
The string length is 5, but sizeof doesn't give that
data.result: Use strlen(s) to get the string length: printf("%zu\n", strlen(s));

narr: Next up is a common confusion between pointers and arrays.
When you declare a pointer with char *s, sizeof gives the pointer size.
On a 64-bit system, this is 8 bytes, not the string length.
To get the string length, you need to use strlen instead.
The fix is simple: use strlen to get the actual string length.
Remember that sizeof on a pointer gives the pointer size,
not the size of what it points to.

data.heading: Problem P3 — String Comparison via ==
steps: The == operator compares array addresses, not contents
a and b are two different objects in memory
The comparison is false even though the strings are identical
String contents should be compared with strcmp
data.result: Use strcmp for string comparison: if (strcmp(a, b) == 0)

narr: This bug shows a fundamental misunderstanding of how strings work.
When you use == with arrays, you're comparing their addresses,
not the actual character contents.
Even if two strings have identical content, they're stored separately.
To compare string contents, you need to use strcmp.

data.heading: Fixed Code for P3

narr: The fix is to use strcmp for proper string comparison.
strcmp returns 0 when the strings are identical,
so we check for equality with 0.

data.heading: Problem P4 — Buffer Too Small for strcpy
steps: The string "hello" requires 6 bytes: 5 letters plus null terminator
dest only holds 5 bytes
strcpy writes one byte beyond the array end
This causes a buffer overflow
data.result: Make the destination buffer large enough: char dest[6];

narr: This is a classic buffer overflow waiting to happen.
The string "hello" needs 6 bytes including the null terminator.
But the destination buffer only has 5 bytes.
When strcpy copies the string, it writes beyond the buffer.
This can corrupt memory and lead to security vulnerabilities.
The fix is simple: make sure the destination buffer is large enough.
Always allocate space for the null terminator when working with strings.

data.heading: Problem P5 — Modifying a String Literal
steps: String literals like "hello" are stored in read-only memory
s merely points to this read-only location
Attempting to modify s[0] tries to write to read-only memory
This typically causes a segmentation fault
data.result: Create a modifiable copy: char s[] = "hello";

narr: This bug demonstrates a dangerous misunderstanding of string literals.
When you write "hello" in code, it's stored in read-only memory.
The pointer s just points to this location.
Trying to modify it through the pointer attempts to write to read-only memory.
This usually results in a segmentation fault crash.
The fix is to create a modifiable copy using an array declaration.
This creates a writable copy of the string in memory.
Now the modification works and prints "Jello".

data.heading: Problem P6 — Returning a Pointer to a Local Variable
steps: buf is a local variable on the greeting() stack frame
The stack frame disappears when greeting() returns
The returned pointer becomes dangling
Reading *g is undefined behavior
data.result: Fix by using a static array, caller-provided buffer, or malloc'd memory

narr: This is a subtle but dangerous bug involving memory lifetimes.
The buffer buf exists on the stack within the greeting function.
When greeting returns, its stack frame is destroyed.
The pointer to buf becomes dangling, pointing to invalid memory.
Using this pointer leads to undefined behavior.

data.heading: Fixed Code for P6 (Static Variant)

narr: One fix is to make the buffer static.
Static variables have a lifetime extending beyond the function call.
This ensures the buffer remains valid when the pointer is returned.
Other solutions include using a buffer provided by the caller,
or using malloc'd memory that the caller will free.
